titre: The Unua Libro (1887): A Book Signed “Dr. Esperanto”
accroche: In 1887, the author calls his language “international” and signs as Dr. Esperanto. The pledge he asks for is worth something only if ten million others sign it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1887, a 42-page book appears in Warsaw from the publisher Chaim Kelter, first in Russian, under the title *Международный язык*, “International Language.” It is signed with a pseudonym: Dr. Esperanto. Behind it, Ludwik Zamenhof. The word that now names the language is not its name there; it is the author's.

## A Name That Comes from a Pseudonym

The project is called there the “international language,” *lingvo internacia* in Esperanto. According to the Wikipedia entry on the *Unua Libro* (“first book”), it is in 1889 that the pseudonym begins to serve as the name of the language: the first speakers fall into the habit of using the pseudonym for the language itself. The entry on the language glosses it as “one who hopes.” The 1889 American translation, by Henry Phillips Jr., one of the secretaries of the American Philosophical Society, is still titled *An Attempt Towards an International Language* and notes that Dr. Esperanto is a pen name.

## A Conditional Pledge

The book asks for neither time nor money for the project. It encloses forms that the reader is invited to sign and send back to Warsaw. The text of the form, in the 1889 translation, commits the signatory to learn the international language proposed by Dr. Esperanto, if it is shown that ten million people have publicly given the same promise. The author insists: signing requires no effort or sacrifice, and commits one to nothing should the enterprise fail, other than to learn the language when ten million others have done so. When the number is reached, he writes, a book will gather all the names and addresses, and the day after its publication the problem will be solved.

Two other notations are provided. Someone who opposes the project can send back the form marked with the word *Kontraŭ* (against), along with his or her objections. Someone who is ready to learn the language without waiting for the others can send it back with an Esperanto word meaning “unconditionally.”

## What This Shifts

Zamenhof also claims a short grammar and a reduced vocabulary: with 900 words learned, he asserts, one knows the language inside and out, since the rules allow all the others to be formed. But it is not linguistics that structures the appeal. An international language is useful only if others speak it, and the ten-million clause treats this problem through coordination: no one is bound to learn alone. The preamble of the book states the aim in these terms: a language that all nations could adopt, the common property of the whole world without belonging to any existing nationality.

The name, for its part, took hold with no form or list of signatures, through the usage of those who spoke the language. A language designed to belong to no nation bears the pseudonym of its author: did the project gain or lose by it?

repere.texte: The form attached to the Unua Libro commits its signatory to learn Dr. Esperanto's international language only if it is shown that ten million people have publicly given the same promise.
repere.source: Zamenhof (writing as Dr. Esperanto), An Attempt Towards an International Language, trans. Henry Phillips Jr., New York, Henry Holt & Company, 1889

carte.punch: Esperanto was first a pseudonym: in 1887, the language was called “international.”
carte.idee: The Unua Libro (Warsaw, 1887) is signed Dr. Esperanto, Zamenhof's pen name. The book proposes a pledge to learn the language that is worth something only if ten million people sign it publicly. The pseudonym became the name of the language from 1889.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: An Attempt Towards an International Language, 1889 translation (in English)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The 1887 book as it was translated in New York, with the pledge form at the end of the volume.

quiz.question: What does the pledge offered to readers of the Unua Libro commit them to?
choix: Learning the language within the following year, regardless of the number of signatories
Learning the language if ten million people publicly promise the same thing
Funding the spread of the language in the Russian Empire through an annual subscription
Teaching the language to ten of their acquaintances before the end of 1887
quiz.explication: The form is conditional: the signatory promises to learn the language only if it is shown that ten million people have given the same promise, and the book specifies that signing commits one to nothing if the enterprise fails. It asks for neither a subscription nor teaching to acquaintances. A separate notation, unconditional, existed only for those who wanted to learn without waiting for the others.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under what title and in what language does the 1887 book appear, before being translated into English in 1889?
choix: In French, under the title “Universal Language”
In German, under the title “Language of Reason”
In Russian, under a title meaning “International Language”
In Polish, under the title “Language of the People”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The book first appears in Russian, under the title Международный язык, which means “International Language,” before the 1889 American translation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the form attached to the book, what can a reader opposed to Zamenhof's project do?
choix: Send back the form unsigned, which automatically counts as a refusal
Write directly to the publisher Chaim Kelter to request that the book be withdrawn
Sign anyway, since no notation on the form provides for refusal
Send back the form marked with the word Kontraŭ, along with his or her objections
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The form provides a separate notation, Kontraŭ (against), which a reader opposed to the project can send back along with objections to the proposed language.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Zamenhof claim about the vocabulary of his language, in the Unua Libro?
choix: That at least ten thousand words are needed to hold a simple conversation
That with 900 words learned, one knows the language inside and out thanks to the formation rules
That the vocabulary remains to be invented, the book proposing only the grammar
That each nation must supply its own vocabulary, only the grammar being common
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Zamenhof asserts that 900 words learned are enough to know the language inside and out, the formation rules allowing all the other words to be built.
